title: Rent guarantee products can open a housing door while leaving the renter with the repayment risk
source_unit: NBER quantitative rent-guarantee model and TheGuarantors public renter/operator descriptions; separate model and provider-document units
geography: United States housing market model and US provider terms, with state availability caveats

observations.period: NBER model; calibrated US housing and income/health shock setting

denominator.unit: quantitative-equilibrium model population and calibrated states; no survey denominator

access_viability.value: unrestricted access is not financially viable; restricted access can restore viability

targeting_split.value: private insurers must target better-off renters to break even, while public insurers focus on households most at risk of homelessness

observations.method: NBER quantitative equilibrium model of rent guarantee insurance after negative income or health-expenditure shocks, including moral hazard and adverse selection; it is not an evaluation of a broad US rollout.
observations.uncertainty: The model's welfare, deposit, and homelessness effects depend on calibration and assumed insurance design. It does not measure actual premiums, take-up, claims, landlord behavior, or later tenant outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Modeled renters and households differentiated by risk and insurance-provider type; exact model groups and calibration govern interpretation.
observations.counterinterpretation: A public insurance design may improve risk sharing but require public funding and targeting; a private product may be available to a renter who can pay while excluding or burdening the highest-risk renter.

observations.period: Current provider terms checked 2026-09-22; TheGuarantors renter and operator descriptions

denominator.unit: provider product terms and FAQs; no approval, take-up, claim, or tenant-outcome denominator

entry_function.value: a renter purchases a lease guarantee to qualify for a home they may not otherwise qualify to rent

premium.value: personalized, upfront, and non-refundable if the lease proceeds

claim_repayment.value: if the provider pays the landlord for covered rent or damage, the renter remains liable to reimburse the provider

availability.value: not every building accepts the product; coverage and pricing vary by state, property, lease, and financial profile

observations.method: Review of the provider's public renter FAQ, operator FAQ, and help page; these are product descriptions, not independent performance data.
observations.uncertainty: Public terms do not show approval rates, premium distribution, claims frequency, repayment success, credit consequences, eviction outcomes, housing stability, or whether the product improved access for a defined renter population.
observations.subgroup: Renters who do not meet a property's usual requirements, including some self-employed, recent-graduate, international, or lower-credit applicants; this is provider-described targeting, not an independently measured subgroup.
observations.counterinterpretation: A landlord-facing guarantee can still help a renter obtain a lease and avoid a larger deposit. A claim being repayable does not prove that every renter experiences it as harmful debt, and provider terms do not establish actual claim frequency.

related_sources.claim: The provider separately states that rent coverage is not monthly tenant relief and that a landlord claim can leave the renter responsible for reimbursement.

boundary: The model and provider documents support a protection-versus-repayment boundary, not a measured tenant outcome. Formal lease access, landlord protection, premium payment, claim payment, renter reimbursement, housing stability, credit, and later exit must remain separate stages. The NBER model is not a rollout evaluation, and the provider documents are not independent evidence of market performance.
